Question: What is a successful Engineering career?
Answer: It depends on how you define success! If you define successful as working as an engineer until you retire, then most engineers are successful. Of course the same standard can be applied to many career. If you work at a job that pays the bills and allows you to retire, then you were a success. Now, some people reserve success at being at the top of the profession. In this case, Steve Wozniak who create the Apple II would be considered a success. Bob Jones who worked at GE for his entire career but was never recognized would not. I personally dont think that way. Nor do I can for those 40 under 40 lists, that follow certain people who seem promising. To to, you have to land in the right spot to start with, and its ignores lost of other equally talented people who flew under the radar. Such thinking is too limiting in my opinion. Now, that does not mean that we should not strive for accomplishments. I have project that I’m proud of, and many other unknown engineers have contributed to amazing things. Think of all of the engineers behind the Apollo project alone! All of them wear success, even if we never heard of them. Here is a illustration and business tip all rolled into one!

Question: What are some reasons why people find it difficult to leave a bad job for a new one, even if the new job appears to be better in every aspect?
Answer: Some people have been burned before. After all, some companies look good from the outside. It's sort of like dating, where both parties are on their best behavior. But once you start, then you lean they want you 12 hours a day, and they learn that you play with you phone all day. Other people fear change. They would rather deal with the devil they know than risk the job being worse (my first point). Keep in mind most people change job due to poor manager, others for better pay, or more exciting projects, But keep in mind that some people find fulfillment outside their job, so that could also be a factor in tolerating an otherwise bad job. Sometimes it's hard to leave a bad job…

Question: Is 40 hours a week of working too much?
Answer: There are a few ways of looking that this… For a lot of the 90’s I worked two jobs. One regular full-time job and a second part-time job. In most cases I put in between 12- and 14-hours a day (the 14-hour day lasted about a year, as later my part-time job was teaching at a local college, and was pretty laid back) The nice thing was that not only was I earning extra income, I was also not spending money trying to entertain myself. Now, non-salary people get paid overtime, which is also nice but can burn you out if it is excessive or extends too long. In my case the jobs were different, so there was a mental “shifting of gears” between jobs. Now, there is a push to create a four-day work week, and that might work of some office jobs. They claim people can get just as much work done in 32 hours as 40. But even if true, will that be sustainable day in and day out, over the long term? And will that create a 2-teir workforce, with people working construction, retail, nursing or manufacturing all continue to work longer (40+) hours?
